subject: MAP: performance benchmark alignment & repro plan
messages:
From: Sarah Blake <sarah.blake@acme.ai>
To: soojin_lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>
Cc: eng-data@acme.ai
Date: 2026-07-10T16:12:00-07:00
Subject: MAP: initial perf results and questions

Hi Soojin,

Thanks for the MAP draft — attached is a short run of the workload we promised for the perf evaluation and the raw CSVs (acme_latency_results.csv). High level: we measured TTFT (time-to-first-token), steady-state throughput, and p50/p95 latencies under our standard harness. Numbers we saw: TTFT ~ 310ms, p50 token latency 18ms, p95 67ms when running at concurrency 8 with batch size 4. Throughput (tokens/sec) ~ 920.

These results are notably worse than Redwood’s public MAP target (TTFT < 200ms, p95 < 40ms) — before we escalate I'd like to capture what we ran so we can align methodology:
- Model: open-llm/opt-13b (float32)
- Runtime: internal harness (node-based) invoking model via HTTP endpoint on A100 (40GB), driver set to single-process multi-threaded.
- Tokenization: custom pre-tokenizer that preserves whitespace, we used max_tokens=1024.
- Warm up: 5 iterations, no KV persistence between requests.
- Metric definitions: TTFT measured from request timestamp to first byte on the wire.

Potential sources of discrepancy from Redwood MAP: hardware differences (A100 gen), batching strategy (we used small batch size), and no persistent KV cache — we didn’t use streaming with early flush. Also we suspect tokenizer mismatch (we saw average input tokenization 12% higher than expectation).

Can you do two things so we can close this MAP quickly:
1) Share the exact Redwood runner command lines, kernel/runtime versions, and batch/concurrency profile used for the MAP example.
2) Suggest a short repro matrix we can run that toggles KV caching, streaming vs non-streaming, and tokenizer pipeline so we can isolate root cause.

We’re aiming to finalize the MAP and close procurement by end of July; if we can converge on methodology this week we’ll update procurement timelines accordingly.

Attachments: acme_latency_results.csv, acme_map_v2.xlsx

Thanks — happy to hop on a quick 30-min call if helpful.

—Sarah
Sarah Blake
Head of Platform Engineering | ACME AI

TTFT reported in MAP measures from request start to first token emitted (includes our runtime scheduling overhead).

Internal plan (cc’ing team):

- Aisha: coordinate MAP doc updates and procurement timeline (if we find delta driven by config differences we’ll propose SLA adjustments).

Sarah — we’ll push a short repro report by end of Monday. If the divergence is primarily tokenizer or harness differences we can remedy without changing pricing; if it’s kernel/hardware then we’ll flag performance tiers in the MAP. Would you be open to a 30-minute alignment call Tuesday morning?

Quick update from repro runs I kicked off this morning and early findings. I put raw logs (karty-runlogs-20260711.txt) into the shared folder. TL;DR: we can reproduce a large portion of the delta by aligning tokenizer and disabling KV cache; remaining gap appears to be harness-level batching differences. Details: 

What I ran:
- Host: Redwood dedicated A100-40GB (same GPU class), OS: Ubuntu 22.04, driver 525.85.05
- Model: open-llm/opt-13b float32; runner: redwood-runner v1.4.2; tokenizers: hf/tokenizers 0.14.4 (match request), batch_size=4, concurrency=8, KV cache disabled (to match Sarah’s run). Warmup: 3 iterations.

Findings:
- Tokenization: when we switched from our default whitespace-preserving pre-tokenizer to hf/tokenizers the input token count dropped ~11% which lowered average token latency by ~9% (p50 reduced from 20ms -> 18ms).
- KV cache: cost of not using KV is visible primarily at TTFT — enabling KV (warm cache) drops TTFT by ~80–120ms depending on model sequence length. That accounts for ~100ms of the 110ms TTFT gap.
- Batching/harness: their harness does single-process HTTP invocations with request-level scheduling that limits throughput; our runner uses continuous batching and async I/O which yields higher throughput at same concurrency. When we forced single-process HTTP semantics we saw throughput drop to ~940 tokens/sec and p95 move up ~10–15ms.

Conclusion / next steps:
1) We can create a short appendix to the MAP that defines two operating modes and expected SLAs: "low-latency KV-enabled" (map default) and "stateless HTTP" (their current harness) with separate performance expectations.
2) Recommend a small change to ACME’s integration (KV warm policy + use of streaming) that should bring them within the MAP TTFT target without infra changes. We should validate with ACME running hf/tokenizers 0.14.4 and the small warm-cache patch.
3) I suggest we run one aligned cross-check together (screen-share) so they can reproduce the change end-to-end and we can accept the MAP.

I’m available for the proposed 2026-07-13 09:00 PT call. Assigning myself to the reproducer write-up; will upload a short delta table by tomorrow morning for Marissa to pull into the MAP delta doc.

—Karthik
Senior Performance Engineer, Redwood Inference
